title: How VS Code Went from Monthly to Weekly Releases with AI — Harald Kirschner
talk_summary: VS Code moved from monthly to weekly releases by treating AI velocity as a systems problem: making the codebase agent-ready, encoding expert knowledge in skills, removing CI/build bottlenecks, and building tight automated feedback loops (component screenshots, Playwright self-verification, mandatory AI code review, automated issue triage to auto-PRs). The core lesson is to fix the next bottleneck in the feedback loop rather than token-maxing.

takeaways.technique: Attack the slowest CI/build step first because agent concurrency compounds it
takeaways.what_they_do: They migrated to TypeScript Go to cut build/lint/CI time, arguing that a slow step is tolerable for one human but becomes a hard throughput ceiling when 10-20 agents all wait on it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: once you hit that with agents, you have 10 agents, 20 agents running and hitting the same bottleneck, these any slow part of your CI/CD will compound
takeaways.numbers: TypeScript Go was a 10x improvement in builds

takeaways.technique: Mandatory AI review gate with risk-tiered effort, humans only after comments resolved
takeaways.what_they_do: An automated reviewer is a mandatory check on every PR, with low/medium/high effort dialed by repo risk; humans do not look at a PR until all review comments are resolved and addressed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if a review after review is done, humans will not even look at PR until all the comments are resolved and and addressed

takeaways.technique: Give agents the ability to run the app and self-verify via browser automation
takeaways.what_they_do: A /launch skill uses Playwright to open VS Code, click through a scenario, capture logs, and validate fixes before/after without a human clicking; plus a component browser that screenshots every component and diffs changes per PR.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If your agent cannot use your application, your product directly to get this feedback loop of is it all working, then that's a really big investment

takeaways.technique: Deterministic triage pipeline feeding an auto-fix multi-agent loop
takeaways.what_they_do: Telemetry is filtered to full error stacks, fingerprinted/bucketed, then issues are filed to area owners and a PR is auto-created by an agent that diagnoses and fixes, with human approval at the end.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have 10 issues filed assigned to specific area owners that a PR is autocreated to actually already try to fix the problem

takeaways.technique: Cheap end-to-end eval harness to measure per-model token cost on your own harness
takeaways.what_they_do: They keep an easy-to-extend eval suite (VSC bench) and ran a trivial 'write hello world' scenario across models, revealing huge token-cost differences on the same task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The same five character file took the most expensive model 70x more tokens and that was not the high reasoning model
takeaways.numbers: 70x more tokens for the same 5-character file on the most expensive model

takeaways.technique: Encode expert knowledge as maintained skills owned by area experts
takeaways.what_they_do: Accessibility best practices were turned into a skill reviewed and maintained by the accessibility owner, so expert input reaches every agent instead of one person being repeatedly pulled in; agents.md files are living documents updated as agents err.
takeaways.evidence_quote: think how you can encode your expert knowledge to unblock this like few users that might be always asked for this input into a skill
